q: The checkout has <div class="btn" onclick="pay()">Pay now</div> next to a real <button>. What did Chromium do with the div?
options: It exposed it as a button, because a click handler is attached to it
Tab skipped it and the accessibility tree showed it as plain text
Tab reached it, but neither Enter nor Space triggered its click handler
It exposed it as a link, because the pointer cursor changes on hover
explain: A click handler adds no role and no focusability: Tab went straight to the next control and the tree listed "text: Pay now". "Tab reached it but keys did nothing" describes a div with role="button" and tabindex="0", which still lacks the keyboard behaviour of a real button.

q: What is the accessible name of <button aria-label="Close">Remove item</button>?
options: "Remove item", because the visible text always wins over attributes
"Remove item Close", because both sources are joined together
"Close", because aria-label comes before the content
No name at all, because the two sources conflict with each other
explain: In the accessible name computation, aria-label comes before naming from content, so Chromium named the button "Close". That is exactly why it is a bug: the visible label is no longer in the name (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name), so a voice control user saying "click Remove item" fails.

q: In the back office SPA, the agent presses Enter on the "Order 42" link. The router removes the old page, link included, and renders the new one. Where is keyboard focus, measured in Chromium?
options: On body, because the focused element was removed
On the new page's h1, moved by the browser
On the first focusable element of the new page
Still on the removed link, which keeps focus while detached
explain: When the focused element leaves the DOM, document.activeElement falls back to body and a screen reader announces nothing. The browser never moves focus to the new heading on its own: that is the job of code such as the PageHeading component, which focuses an h1 with tabindex="-1".

q: A button is styled with button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid }. Which interaction showed the outline in Chromium?
options: A mouse click on the button
Any focus, whatever the input device
Only a programmatic button.focus() after a mouse click
Reaching the button with Tab or Shift+Tab
explain: Measured: keyboard focus matched :focus-visible, while a mouse click on the same button focused it without matching. Browsers use heuristics so that keyboard users always see focus and mouse users clicking a button do not, which is why styling :focus-visible beats deleting the outline.

q: Which of these does a <dialog> opened with showModal() NOT do by default, measured in Chromium?
options: Move focus to the first focusable element inside it
Close when the user presses Escape
Close when the user clicks the backdrop
Remove the rest of the page from the accessibility tree
explain: A backdrop click left the dialog open; light dismiss needs closedby="any", which MDN still lists as limited availability. Focus moving in, Escape closing it and the page behind leaving the accessibility tree were all measured as default behaviour of showModal().

q: A filters drawer opens over the orders table. A developer puts aria-hidden="true" on the table's container. What happens to the "Delete order" button inside it?
options: It leaves the accessibility tree but Tab still reaches it
It leaves the accessibility tree and the Tab order, like inert does
It stays in the accessibility tree but can no longer be clicked
Nothing changes: aria-hidden only applies to images and icons
explain: Measured in Chromium: the button disappeared from the accessibility tree, yet Tab focused it, so a screen reader user lands on a control with no name. Removing it from the Tab order and from clicks is what inert does, and that is the attribute to use behind an overlay.

q: In the OrderTabs component, the "History" tab is selected. What are the tabIndex values of Details, Payments and History?
options: 0, 0, 0, so that the Tab key visits every tab in turn
-1, -1, 0: only the selected tab is in the Tab sequence
-1, -1, -1, and the tablist container itself has tabindex 0
1, 2, 3, so that the Tab key follows the visual order of tabs
explain: This is the roving tabindex: one tab has tabindex 0 and the others -1, so the whole list is one Tab stop and the arrow keys move between tabs. Measured after pressing End: Details -1, Payments -1, History 0. Positive tabindex values must never be used.

q: What does role="status" give the cart announcer?
options: An assertive live region that interrupts whatever the screen reader says
Focus moves to the message element each time its text changes
A landmark that users can jump to from the screen reader landmarks menu
A polite live region: changes are announced when the user is idle
explain: role="status" is a live region with polite announcements by default; role="alert" is the assertive one. A live region announces changes without moving focus, which is exactly what a cart update needs.

q: Grey #777777 on white has a contrast ratio of 4.48:1. Where may it be used under WCAG 1.4.3 (AA)?
options: Anywhere, because 4.48 rounds up to the 4.5 threshold
Nowhere, because grey text on white always fails the criterion
Only for large text: about 24 px, or 18.5 px bold
Only for body text, because headings need 7:1 at level AA
explain: Normal text needs at least 4.5:1, and 4.48 is below it: thresholds are not rounded. Large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold) needs 3:1, so 4.48 passes there. #767676 on white, at 4.54:1, is the lightest grey of that form that passes for all text.

q: After an RGAA audit, 60% of the applicable criteria are validated. Which mention goes into the accessibility declaration?
options: "Partiellement conforme", since it is at least 50%
"Non conforme", because anything under 100% is non-conformant
"Totalement conforme", because a majority of criteria is met
No mention at all: only public bodies publish a declaration
explain: The RGAA defines "totalement conforme" when every criterion is met, "partiellement conforme" from 50%, and "non conforme" below 50% or without a valid audit. "Non conforme under 100%" is the common confusion; the declaration also lists non-accessible content and a contact.

q: Which problem can an axe scan of the checkout detect on its own?
options: An alt text that describes the wrong product
An input that has no accessible name
A focus order that jumps from the postcode to the footer
A refund dialog that does not return focus on close
explain: A missing name is a fact a rule can check in the DOM. Whether an alt text is right, whether the order of focus makes sense, and what happens after an interaction need a human or a behaviour test, which is why the module adds a focus test and manual passes.

q: With @layer base, components;, base contains #checkout button { color: red } and components contains .pay-button { color: green }. What colour is the Pay button?
options: Red, because an id selector is more specific than a class selector
Red, because base is declared first and keeps priority
It depends on which of the two rules comes last in the file
Green: a later layer wins whatever the specificity
explain: Layers are compared before specificity: the later layer, components, wins. Measured in Chromium, the button was green. Specificity only decides between declarations of the same layer, which is what makes layers useful against legacy id selectors.

q: Code review on the storefront. Which change do you ask for?
options: Add role="button" and tabIndex={0} to the div so keyboards reach it
Add aria-label="Pay" so that screen readers can announce a name
Replace the div with <button type="button">
Add an onKeyDown handler that calls onPay when Enter is pressed
explain: A native button brings the role, focusability, Enter and Space activation, the disabled state and form behaviour. Role and tabindex alone left Enter and Space doing nothing in Chromium, and an Enter handler still misses Space; aria-label would only name a control that keyboard users cannot reach.

q: What name does Chromium compute for the button?
options: "Delivery address"
"Edit address"
"Edit"
"Edit address Delivery address"
explain: aria-labelledby comes first in the accessible name computation and overrides both aria-label and the content: measured, button "Delivery address". The tempting "Edit address" would be right only without aria-labelledby.

q: A voice control user says "click Remove item" on a cart line and nothing happens, while a mouse click works. The markup is <button aria-label="Close">Remove item</button>. What is the cause?
options: Voice control only activates links, so the button must become a link
The name is "Close", so the spoken label matches nothing
The button needs tabindex="0" before voice control can reach it
Voice control reads the title attribute, and this button has none
explain: aria-label replaced the visible text in the name, and voice control matches what the user can see. WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name requires the visible text to be part of the name. A button is already focusable, so tabindex changes nothing here.

q: The back office is a React SPA. Which fix would you ship so that screen reader users notice a page change?
options: Put aria-live="assertive" on main so the new page is read out
Call document.body.focus() after each navigation to reset focus
Give the h1 of every page tabindex="0" so Tab reaches it
Update the title and focus the new h1 (tabindex="-1")
explain: Focusing the heading makes the screen reader read it and makes the next Tab start there (measured). tabindex="-1" allows focus() without adding the heading to the Tab order, whereas tabindex="0" would add a useless Tab stop on every page. An assertive live region around main turns every content update into an interruption, which MDN advises against.

q: With the RefundDialog of section 4 open, the agent presses Escape. What happens, measured with React 19 in Chromium?
code:
<dialog ref={dialogRef} aria-labelledby={titleId}
  onClose={(event) => onClose(event.currentTarget.returnValue === 'confirm')}>
  ...
  <form method="dialog">
    <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
    <button value="confirm">Refund</button>
  </form>
</dialog>
options: The dialog closes, onClose(false) runs and focus returns to the trigger
Nothing, because the component does not handle onCancel
The dialog closes but the parent state stays open, since no prop changed
The dialog closes and onClose(true) runs, since no button was clicked
explain: Escape fires cancel and then close; the close event reaches onClose with an empty returnValue, so confirmed is false and the parent sets open to false. Focus went back to the Refund trigger. onCancel is only needed to prevent closing, and true requires the button with value "confirm".

q: The storefront's mobile menu is a custom panel, not a dialog. When it is open, how do you stop Tab and clicks from reaching the page behind it?
options: Set pointer-events: none on the page behind
Set aria-hidden="true" on the page behind
Set the inert attribute on the page behind
Set tabindex="-1" on every link of the page behind
explain: inert removes its subtree from the Tab order, from clicks and from the accessibility tree in one attribute (measured, and Baseline since April 2023). aria-hidden hides content from screen readers but Tab still reaches it, pointer-events only blocks the mouse, and tabindex on every link misses buttons, inputs and the tree.

q: For the search autocomplete, why does the APG use aria-activedescendant rather than a roving tabindex?
options: Because options inside a listbox are not allowed to receive focus
Because DOM focus must stay in the input while the user types
Because a roving tabindex cannot be implemented with React state
Because aria-activedescendant scrolls the active option into view for free
explain: The combobox pattern keeps DOM focus on the text input while aria-activedescendant tells assistive technology which option is active. The scrolling claim is backwards: the APG says that with aria-activedescendant you must scroll the active option into view yourself, while roving tabindex gets it from focus().

q: In the OrderTabs component, focus is on the selected "Payments" tab and the user presses Tab. Where does focus go?
options: To the "History" tab, the next one in the list
Back to the first tab, "Details"
To the next focusable element after the whole tabs block
To the Payments tab panel, which has tabIndex={0}
explain: The tab list is a single Tab stop, so Tab leaves it; the next stop is the visible panel, focusable because the APG asks for tabindex 0 when the panel starts with non-focusable content (measured). Arrow keys, not Tab, move between tabs.

q: Screen reader users report that "Added to cart" is never announced. What is the most likely bug?
options: The region appears with its text, before it could be registered
role="status" is not a live region by itself; it needs aria-live too
Live regions only announce text that is set through innerHTML
The paragraph must receive focus before a screen reader reads it
explain: MDN advises establishing the live region first, empty, and changing its content later; the most reliable way is to have it in the initial markup. This component mounts the region and its message in the same render. role="status" is a polite live region by default, so the second option is wrong.

q: On mobile checkout, an 80 px fixed "Pay" bar covers fields as the user tabs down the form. Which criterion and fix?
options: 1.4.10 Reflow; switch the bar from fixed to position: sticky
2.5.8 Target Size; make each field taller than the 80 px bar
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured; add scroll padding and end-of-page room
2.4.7 Focus Visible; give the focused fields a thicker outline
explain: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), new in WCAG 2.2, fails when author content entirely hides the focused component. Measured: scroll-padding-bottom fixed every field but the last, and padding at the end of the page fixed that one. A thicker outline is useless when the field itself is under the bar.

q: Which statement about the shop's legal position in France is correct?
options: Only companies with over 250 million euros of turnover in France are obliged
Since 28 June 2025 e-commerce must be accessible, micro-enterprises aside
The obligation only starts with RGAA 5, planned for the end of 2026
The obligation only covers shops whose customers include public bodies
explain: The European Accessibility Act, transposed in France, has covered e-commerce since 28 June 2025; per the DGCCRF, providers with fewer than 10 employees and under 2 million euros are exempt. The 250 million threshold is the older Article 47 rule, which still applies but is not the only one.

q: An interviewer asks what WCAG 2.2 changed compared with 2.1. Which answer is accurate?
options: It replaced the A, AA and AAA levels with a single score out of 100
It raised the AA contrast minimum for body text from 4.5:1 to 7:1
It made every AAA criterion mandatory for public sector websites
It added nine criteria, such as Target Size, and dropped 4.1.1 Parsing
explain: WCAG 2.2 (October 2023) kept the 2.1 criteria, removed 4.1.1 Parsing as obsolete, and added nine criteria, six of them at A or AA. 7:1 is the AAA contrast level (1.4.6), unchanged, and the A, AA and AAA levels remain.

q: Your Playwright test runs axe with the WCAG 2.2 AA tags on /checkout and passes. What can you honestly claim?
options: The checkout now conforms to WCAG 2.2 level AA
The checkout would pass an RGAA audit by an external firm
No violation those rules detect, in the states scanned
Screen reader users can complete a purchase from start to end
explain: A scan checks only what its rules can decide, in the states present at scan time: a closed dialog or an error state is not scanned. Deque itself claims about 57% of issues on average, and Playwright's docs say automated tests cannot detect all WCAG violations, so conformity needs manual testing too.

q: You have time for three screen reader passes before the audit. Which set covers the RGAA test environment and most real users?
options: NVDA + Firefox, VoiceOver + Safari on iOS, TalkBack + Chrome
JAWS + Internet Explorer, VoiceOver + Chrome on macOS, Narrator + Edge
Three runs of axe, in Chrome, in Firefox and in Safari
NVDA with Chrome three times, at 100%, 200% and 400% zoom
explain: The RGAA test environment names NVDA with Firefox on desktop, VoiceOver with Safari and TalkBack with Chrome on mobile, and WebAIM's 2026 survey shows VoiceOver on 72.2% of mobile setups. Rule engines are not screen readers, and a single pairing misses mobile entirely.

q: What colour is the Pay button, measured in Chromium?
options: rgb(0, 0, 255), because unlayered styles always beat layered ones
rgb(1, 1, 1): important reverses the layer order
rgb(2, 2, 2), because components is the later of the two layers
rgb(0, 0, 255), because it is the last declaration in the file
explain: For !important declarations the order is reversed: earlier layers beat later ones, and layered important beats unlayered important. Measured: rgb(1, 1, 1). "Unlayered beats layers" is true only for normal declarations, which is the trap here.

q: Which rule colours the Pay button?
options: Green, because four classes add up to more than one id
Green, because it comes later in the file
Both apply and the browser blends them
Red, because one id outweighs any number of classes
explain: Specificity is compared column by column: (1,1,0) against (0,4,0), and the id column decides before classes are counted. Measured in Chromium: red. Source order only matters when specificity is equal.

q: The Filters menu has z-index: 9999 but opens under the sticky header (z-index: 10). Its toolbar has transform: translateZ(0). Which fix works?
options: Raise the menu to z-index: 99999 so it beats the header
Add position: relative to the menu so z-index applies
Make the menu a popover (top layer)
Add isolation: isolate to the toolbar to reset stacking
explain: The transform makes the toolbar a stacking context, so the menu's z-index only competes inside it. A popover is drawn in the top layer, above the header (measured). Any child z-index fails, and isolation: isolate creates the same kind of context, so the menu stayed under the header in that test too.

q: A developer adds container-type: inline-size to an inline-block wrapper around a product card, and the card disappears. Why?
options: Container queries only work on elements inside a grid layout
It cannot size from its content, so it shrinks to 0
Inline-size containment hides any content that overflows it
The @container rule needs a container name to match anything
explain: Inline-size containment means the container is sized as if it had no content; a shrink-to-fit element such as an inline-block then measured 0 px wide in Chromium. Give the container a width from outside, for example a block or a grid track. Unnamed @container rules match the nearest container, so the name is not the problem.
